author: Claude
message:
Make the SDR decision deterministic, and the model advisory in fact

Section 10 asks that qualification not collapse to IDEAL / NOT_IDEAL and that
no model grant outbound authority. The evidence layer landed in #98; the
decision on top of it did not exist, so nothing enforced either half.

A prospect is scored across nine weighted dimensions, each carrying its own
provenance, and a deterministic policy reads those numbers to pick one of
four dispositions. A model assessment enters as one input with
MODEL_INFERENCE provenance, capped at half weight where no observation
exists, and it can never carry icpFit, buyerRoleFit or reachability on its
own -- those must be source-backed before a prospect enters an experiment.
Reachability is not scored at all: it is read off the verified routes.

A model that includes a decision-shaped field -- disposition, outboundAuthority,
suppressionOverride, budgetCents -- does not have that field ignored. The
prospect is quarantined and the requested fields are named, because a model
reaching for authority is itself a finding.

The policy reads numbers and states, never prose, which is what makes
instructions embedded in a prospect's own copy inert rather than merely
discouraged. There is a test that drives exactly that.

ELIGIBLE_FOR_EXPERIMENT means the governed send path may now consider this
prospect. It is not permission to contact anybody, and the result says so.

Section 29's invariant is a hostile scenario: someone unsubscribes, a later

once observed it dominates, whatever arrives later.

buyer+newsletter@example.com was treated as a different person from
buyer@example.com, and on Gmail so was b.uyer@. Suppression matches on the
address as the receiving mailbox sees it -- lowercased, plus-tag stripped,
dots removed only on domains that ignore them. Over-matching costs a lead;
under-matching costs a complaint we were told not to earn.

A complaint recorded as a riskFlag rather than a state did not block at all.
Refusal flags now block as firmly as the state does, while ordinary
deliverability flags like role-account still do not.

author: Claude
message:
Make a cycle that died mid-flight count as the failure it was

A mesh cycle writes STARTED, does its work, then writes TERMINAL. If the
process dies in between, the fail-closed half already worked: that occurrence
can never be re-delivered, so no consequence happens twice.

The other half was silent. Founder-absence readiness is derived from terminal
receipts, so a cycle that never reached TERMINAL was not a failed tick -- it
was nothing at all. A mesh crashing every other cycle could present an
unbroken run of healthy cycles and certify a seven-day absence on it. The
probe that found this ran twenty clean cycles alongside six crashes and
reported failedTicks: 0.

Readiness now refuses to certify while any abandoned cycle is outstanding,
and the count is a required dimension of a supplied proof, like open dead
letters -- a caller cannot certify by omitting it. reconcileAbandonedAgentMeshCycles
turns an abandoned STARTED receipt into a durable DEGRADED terminal receipt
so the crash is written down; it replays no work. The scheduler runs it at
the top of each cycle, and refuses to start a cycle it could not run, since
the history it is about to add to would be unsound.

A cycle still inside its horizon is presumed running, not abandoned.

Also brings three readiness assertions onto the duration-proof semantics
#96/#97 introduced. One of them asserted that eleven capability booleans and
no observation window reach KILIMANJARO_READY, which is the one-shot boolean
issue #83 exists to remove; it now pins the opposite.

author: Claude
message:
Give the scheduler a window the starved runs are actually in

PR #94 adds a durable selection ledger so the scheduler serves the
least-recently-selected active run first, and that part works. But the
active-run scan it orders is itself bounded at 200, and it was taken
newest-updated-first. Ticking a run refreshes its updatedAt, so served runs
stayed at the front of that window and any run past the cap never entered
it. With 260 active runs and five times the capacity needed, sixty were
never served once -- fair ordering inside a window the starved work is not
in is not fairness.

listLatestAutonomyRuns takes an explicit order; the scheduler asks for
oldest-touched first, so being served moves a run out of the window and
being ignored moves it in. Ties are broken on runId rather than left to the
sort's discretion, so one cohort cannot win every cycle. Operator-facing
callers keep newest-first.

The regression drives issue #85's actual claim -- every still-active run is
served within a bounded number of cycles, for N greater than the scan cap,
across a restart -- and fails on the previous ordering.

author: Claude
message:
Make a zero-effect claim prove itself, and teach the scanner the third ledger name

PR #92 routes every autonomy worker result through the relay's validResult
before it can move a run. Two things were wrong underneath that.

An omitted ledger key read as zero, because the check was
Number(ledger[key] || 0). A worker could therefore assert 'no external
effects' by shipping {} -- silence scored exactly the same as a signed zero.
A NaN scored zero too (NaN is falsy), and an array passed as an object.
The ledger must now carry the canonical key set with real numeric zeros, and
an invented counter is reported as an unknown effect key rather than as a
credential leak, which is what the secret scanner had been calling it.

The scanner exempts ledger fields from the credential pattern, because a
ledger's own key is called credentialChanges. It listed two of the three
field names this codebase writes; results carrying a businessEffectLedger
were rejected as secret-bearing. Both ledger shapes and the full list of

Fail closed on constraint overflow instead of dropping a parent's rules

PR #91 enforces that a child task inherits every constraint its parent
carries, but at the ceiling it broke its own invariant. compileTaskIntent
trimmed the incoming list to MAX_CONSTRAINTS - 2 and then prepended the two
mandatory constraints. A parent already holding the full 64 (62 of its own
plus the two mandatory) therefore produced a child with 62: the last two
parent restrictions vanished silently, which is exactly the disappearance
the monotonicity rule exists to prevent.

Compile the complete set once and refuse when it overflows. A task now
either carries every constraint it was handed or it does not compile.

author: mohammedwessam2007
message:
Make relay dispatch idempotent, so a crash mid-dispatch cannot pay twice (#89)

Making the mesh reachable made a real bug reachable too, and finding it was
only possible because the path now exists.

agent-autonomy-pump dispatches a task to the relay, and only afterwards does
agent-autonomy-job persist the run carrying the relayRef. Everything between
those two lines is a window in which the relay task exists and the run does not
know it -- a crash, an OOM, a container reclaim, or a failed snapshot write all
land in it.

createGithubRelayTask created a GitHub issue unconditionally. So the next tick
re-dispatched the same deterministic taskId and a SECOND issue appeared for one
task. Two workers claim two issues, do the work twice, and with provider-backed
workers that is two charges.

Reproduced directly before fixing: same input twice, two issues, one taskId.

The transport is now idempotent on taskId against open, not-done relay issues.
Four cases, each with its own answer:

- retry after a crash returns ALREADY_QUEUED and the existing issue number, so
  the run rebinds instead of re-dispatching. A distinct status, not a silent
  QUEUED: nothing was created, and a receipt saying otherwise is a lie an audit
  trail carries forever.
- the same id with different content is refused. Returning either version would
  be a guess about which caller is right.
- a task that already completed and closed may be dispatched again.
  Deduplication must not become a permanent ban on re-running an objective.
- a client that cannot list issues is refused outright, because it cannot tell a
  first dispatch from a retry, and creating on that assumption is exactly the
  unknown consequential state that must not proceed.

Identity comparison deliberately excludes createdAt, status and deadline. A
retry is by definition a second compilation at a later instant, so comparing
whole tasks would report every legitimate recovery as a conflict.

One further refusal, for the case that is neither "duplicate" nor "no
duplicate": if the first page of open relay tasks comes back full, an unscanned
page may hold the duplicate, and that is "cannot tell", not "none found". Fifty
concurrent open relay tasks is far past any expected load so it should never
fire, but reporting "cannot tell" as "none found" is precisely how a duplicate
charge slips through.

The regression test drops the post-dispatch run on the floor exactly as a killed
process would and asserts one issue exists after two ticks. Verified it fails
against the previous code by reverting the fix and re-running.

Gate: 360 files parse, 1603 tests, 1561 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped (unchanged,
all gated on a real Postgres), relay-safety 150/150, 0 vulnerabilities, lite/
untouched. No provider was called and no money was spent.

author: mohammedwessam2007
message:
Make the agent mesh reachable, and put the activation gate in front of it (#88)

* Give the agent mesh an entry point, and the two functions it needs to run

agent-mesh-control-plane composes the autonomy pump and the model workers
into a bounded cycle. It is the top of the cognitive bus, twenty-six modules
sit underneath it, and outside tests/ nothing imported it. No scheduler job,
no worker handler, no npm script, no workflow.

It was worse than unscheduled. runAgentMeshCycle requires an adapterFactory
and a compileRelayTask, and neither existed outside a test file: the only
adapterFactory in the repository was the stub `() => ({})` in a unit test,
and compileRelayTaskFromIntent was written, tested, and never passed to
anything. The first time an entry point existed, the cycle returned BLOCKED
with ["adapter-factory-required", "relay-task-compiler-required"].

chatgpt-relay-client -- the only implementation of the transport shape the
pump wants -- had no non-test importers either. Three complete, tested,
unreachable modules. A green suite does not distinguish "works" from "cannot
be reached", and 1535 passing tests said nothing about this.

Adds:

- scripts/agent-mesh-tick.mjs, one finite invocation. Bounded, non-resident,
  cloud-neutral, disabled unless AGENT_MESH_ENABLED is exactly "true".
  Distinct exit codes so a scheduler can tell DEGRADED from BLOCKED from a
  crash from the normal disabled resting state.
- src/agent-relay-adapter-factory.mjs, the adapterFactory the control plane
  actually means: a memoized chatgpt-relay-client per origin/target pair.
- src/agent-model-executor-factory.mjs, each worker's modelExecutor from its
  declared provider.

The two factories are named apart on purpose. I conflated them first time
through -- "adapterFactory" reads like the thing that talks to a model, and
it is not; it is the wire the compiled task travels over. The control plane
takes both.

A worker config arriving as JSON cannot carry a function, which is why the
tick script has to resolve both and attach them. Until now there was no way
to configure a worker from outside the process at all.

Refusals kept deliberate: a provider without both a pricing source and a
verification date is refused, because cost computed from unsourced pricing is
a number the system invented and the compute ledger would be quietly
fictional. A worker whose provider cannot be configured fails the tick by
name rather than being skipped -- silently doing nothing is
indistinguishable from having no work.

tests/agent-mesh-entry-point.test.mjs seeds a real autonomy run, drives a
real cycle through the real compiler and the real adapter over a stub fetch,
and asserts the task reached the transport and the relayRef was persisted. It
also asserts the cycle still fails closed with a dependency missing, so this
wiring cannot be deleted without a test noticing.

Writing that test found something worth keeping: the first version invented
its own externalEffectLedger shape and the client rejected it. It now imports
the real ZERO_EFFECTS. A stub that imitates a contract instead of importing
it will eventually disagree with it.

No business-world authority is added. Every task the cycle compiles stays
LOCAL_PREPARATION and businessEffectAuthority stays NONE.

Gate: 357 files parse, 1577 tests, 1535 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped (unchanged,
all gated on a real Postgres), relay-safety 150/150, 0 vulnerabilities,
lite/ untouched.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01ARPWEE3rEGQ8PZMzcMuaCX

* Enforce the activation gate, reach the sandbox provider, name the canonical spend path

Three more modules that were complete, tested, and unreachable.

The activation gate was the important one. agent-mesh-activation-gate decides
whether the mesh may call a model provider at all, and nothing ever built the
evidence input it takes -- so it had no callers, and the entry point added in
the previous commit would have called a provider with nothing between it and
the money.

It is now evaluated on every tick and enforced. Its four permitted modes map
onto worker execution, because a worker tick is the only thing in a cycle that
can call a provider: NO_PROVIDER_CALLS and SYNTHETIC_ONLY run none,
ONE_PROVIDER_CANARY runs one on a canary-ready provider,
BOUNDED_CLOUD_REHEARSAL runs all. Autonomy pumping is unaffected -- it relays
LOCAL_PREPARATION tasks and calls nothing.

agent-mesh-activation-evidence builds the gate's input from two sources kept
deliberately apart. First-hand facts the process checks itself -- is a
credential present, is pricing evidence present -- are always computed and can
never be overridden. Attested claims it cannot verify come from an operator
JSON file. A file cannot upgrade a first-hand fact, or the evidence file
becomes a way to talk the gate into opening; there is a test for that exact
attack. With no file at all the verdict is ARCHITECTURE_ONLY /
NO_PROVIDER_CALLS, which is the intended resting state. A file that is named
but missing or malformed is a refusal, not a fallback: a broken attestation
must not produce the same outcome as never having written one.

Withheld workers exit 3 rather than 0. A scheduler running happily forever
while the workers it was configured to drive never run once is the same silent
failure this entry point exists to remove.

claude-code-sandbox-executor is now the third provider. It drives a local
Claude Code CLI in an isolated sandbox and needs no pricing evidence, because
the CLI reports its own usage and total cost -- the number comes from the tool
that spent it. When the CLI reports no cost the executor returns UNCERTAIN
rather than zero, so unknown spend never looks free. It is a local process, not
free compute; it consumes whatever account it is configured against. It
requires an OS isolation receipt attesting an ephemeral filesystem, no mounted
business credentials, no reachable production network, and Anthropic-only
egress, and the executor rejects a receipt whose root does not match the
configured one. The gate scores only the two API providers, so a sandbox worker
has no canary readiness to look up and is never eligible under
ONE_PROVIDER_CANARY -- unknown reads as not-permitted, asserted by a test.

agent-provider-execution implements the same reserve/invoke/commit transaction
as agent-worker-runtime, with the same uncertainty rule, and had no importers.
The runtime is canonical: same transaction plus durable persistence, lease
heartbeating, and execution records. The duplicate is marked SUPERSEDED rather
than deleted -- it is the clearest small statement of the compute-safety rule
and its tests pin that rule independently -- and a test now fails if anything
outside tests/ imports it. Two reachable implementations of "spend money" is
the shape that produces a double charge.

Also adds scripts/kilimanjaro-manifest.mjs, which measures its own numbers from
the repository instead of restating typed ones, and reports the suite as
NOT_RUN unless handed real TAP output.

Docs: AGENT_MESH_ENTRY_POINT covers the gate and the providers,
AGENT_MESH_REACHABILITY_TRIAGE accounts for all seventeen remaining modules
with no non-test importer (seven are operator tooling where that is correct;
six are business modules gated by tonight's zero external-effect ledger; the
rest name the specific blocker), and KILIMANJARO_ZERO_GAP_OVERNIGHT_REPORT
states plainly what was not done -- notably that the mesh is reachable but has
never been observed doing real work, and that the durable engineering executor
cannot be wired without first writing sandbox provisioning that does not exist.

Gate: 359 files parse, 1597 tests, 1555 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped (unchanged,
all gated on a real Postgres), relay-safety 150/150, 0 vulnerabilities, lite/
untouched. No provider was called and no money was spent.

A self-referential node_modules symlink was committed to main in d806f71, one

so npm cannot run a script and every test fails with module-not-found.

author: Claude
message:
Untrack the node_modules symlink I committed, and close the gap that let it in

A self-referential symlink -- node_modules -> /home/user/uberbondd/node_modules
-- was committed to main in d806f71, one of my own commits. I created it with
a worktree setup line that ran once with the working directory back at the
repository root, then swept it into git with `git add -A`.

Any checkout of that commit gets a node_modules that points at itself. It
shadows the real dependency tree, so npm cannot run a single script and every
test dies with module-not-found. That is what I spent the last hour
misdiagnosing as npm refusing over-long script strings; the scripts were fine.

Two things had to be wrong for this to reach main, and both are now fixed.

The symlink is untracked (`git rm --cached`, so nobody's working copy is
touched).

And .gitignore said `node_modules/` with a trailing slash. That pattern
matches a DIRECTORY. A symlink named node_modules is not a directory, so it
was never ignored and `git add -A` picked it up without complaint. The slash
is gone, which matches both.

Verified after removing the bad link and reinstalling: check:syntax 353 files
parse, 1567 tests, 1525 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped, npm audit 0 vulnerabilities.

author: Claude
message:
Discover the test and syntax suites instead of listing them

Start with the correction, because I got the diagnosis wrong first.

After merging five PRs, `npm run check:syntax` and `npm run test:deterministic`
both exited 216 having executed nothing. I concluded the package.json script
strings had grown too long for npm and rewrote them. That was wrong. The real
cause was mine: a worktree setup line, `ln -sfn .../node_modules node_modules`,
ran once with the working directory back at the repository root and replaced
node_modules with a symlink to itself. Every dependency was gone, so npm could
not run any script at all -- including a script that was literally
`node -e 'console.log("plain ok")'`. Removing the bad link and reinstalling
fixed it. main was green the whole time.

The refactor still earns its place, on evidence rather than on the story that
motivated it:

  old hand-maintained list   116 files named, 135 reached, 1417 tests
  discovered                 126 files handed, 145 reached, 1567 tests

Ten test files had never executed under the main gate -- not by name and not
by import from anything named:

  pending-relay-reconciliation, relay-deployment-attempt,
  relay-deployment-eligibility, relay-preview-integration,
  relay-preview-proof, relay-preview-runbook, relay-shadow-binding,
  relay-vercel-api-executor, relay-vercel-api-request,
  relay-zero-effects-contract

They arrived with #45, which put them in a separate test:relay-safety script
that `npm run check` never calls. Discovery finds them because they exist,
rather than because someone remembered to append them to a 4,496-character
line. That is +150 tests, all passing, that the gate was silently skipping.

The runner also excludes any file another handed file imports, so the
double-execution bug I introduced earlier tonight is now structurally
impossible rather than merely fixed once.

The build-wiring guard is rewritten around the same primitives: every test
file must execute somewhere, none may execute twice, the browser and
live-database suites must stay out of the deterministic set, and no script may
drift back toward the size that is hard to reason about. The size check is
explicitly a canary, set at 2,000 characters -- loose enough not to fail
test:relay-safety at a legitimate 412, since inventing a rule is not the same
as protecting an invariant.

1567 tests, 1525 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped; npm audit 0 vulnerabilities.

author: mohammedwessam2007
message:
Add bounded autonomous GPT ↔ Claude work mesh (#40)

The agent mesh, plus the overnight hardening pass on it.

Five defects were found and fixed by attacking it rather than reading it, two
of them P0:

- A terminal execution record could be resurrected. "Latest" was decided by a
  wall-clock stamp, so two writes in one millisecond were unordered and the
  guard compared against the older record; the terminal state was lost.
- A compute budget could roll back to less spend. Same mistake, but the state
  is money: 700 cents committed loaded back as 0 committed and full capacity
  available.
- Safe retry did not exist: a reservation released without spending anything
  permanently blocked its own task.
- A task declaring no consequence class was accepted and reserved compute;
  unknown consequential state now fails closed.
- A crash-recovery replay was rejected because its keys arrived in a different
  order.

Three of those were one error in three files -- "latest" meaning most recently
stamped rather than furthest along a monotonic quantity. All five sites with
that shape are now resolved: three fixed, two proven safe with the reason
recorded.

Also corrects a mistake made during the pass: 23 test files were reported as
orphaned and wired in, but agent-relay.test.mjs already imports 19 of them, so
the wiring made those run twice and inflated the count. Reverted, and the
build-wiring guard now follows the import graph and catches double-listing in
both directions.

Every fix verified by reverting it and confirming the matching test fails.
Two adversarial sweeps with different mental models found no new P0/P1, and
both are kept as tests/agent-mesh-adversarial-sweep.test.mjs.

Verified: check:syntax passes over 150 modules, 1393 tests, 1351 pass, 0 fail,
42 skipped, npm audit 0 vulnerabilities.

No provider was ever called. No external effect: no sends, spend, deployments,
DNS, credential changes or production mutations. lite/ untouched. GitHub

about this diff.

author: Claude
message:
Keep the adversarial sweeps as tests, and close the matrix

Two sweeps were run against the guards added this session, with deliberately
different mental models: a malicious model sending hostile payloads, then a
hostile scheduler against a stale store.

Sweep 1 produced two findings and neither was a defect. One was my own probe
using an incomplete task fixture, so every case in that block failed for
valid-claimed-relay-task-required rather than for the reason I was testing.
The other is that reserveCompute coerces a numeric string -- "10" becomes 10 --
which is lenient but still passes isSafeInteger and every budget bound, so no
capacity can be created. Both are recorded in the matrix as accepted behaviour
rather than quietly dropped, because a finding that turns out to be nothing is
still worth being able to look up.

Sweep 2 found nothing. It attacked specifically the new guards: a stale write
arriving later in the log, two different terminal statuses at one instant, a

author: Claude
message:
Close the last two ordering gaps: autonomy run state is now protected, not just ordered

The previous report listed these as known-open. They are the fourth and fifth
instance of one mistake, and the pattern is now fully swept.

P1: listLatestAutonomyRuns deduplicated per run with `rowTime > currentTime` --
strictly greater, so a timestamp tie kept the FIRST row seen, which is the
older snapshot. That is not cosmetic: agent-autonomy-job reads this listing to
choose which runs to sweep, so a stale status can put a finished run back into
the active set and have its work redone.

P2 (previously recorded as an open gap): saveAutonomyRunSnapshot enforced no
transition guard at all. Any snapshot was accepted, including one that moved a
run backwards. Run state was ordered but not protected.

Both are closed with the run's own `sequence`, which the pump only ever
increments, so it is a real monotonic authority rather than a guess:

  - a lower sequence is refused as autonomy-run-sequence-regression
  - the same sequence with identical content is an idempotent crash replay
  - the same sequence with different content is autonomy-run-snapshot-conflict,
    because two writers disagreeing about one point in a run must not be
    silently appended
  - loading and listing both rank on sequence first

One existing test had to change. It saved two different run states at the same
sequence by hand and relied on the later one silently overwriting the earlier.
The real pump never produces that -- every advancing path goes through
`next.sequence += 1` -- so the fixture was corrected to advance the sequence,
which preserves what the test was actually checking (the listing dedups to the
latest) while matching how the system behaves. No gate was weakened; a gate was
added, and the new conflict case is now covered explicitly.

The two remaining sites from the previous report were reviewed and are safe,
with the reason recorded rather than assumed:

  - agent-code-artifact-store rejects any digest divergence as
    artifact-identity-collision BEFORE the sort, so every candidate row is
    byte-identical content and the tie only affects provenance metadata.
  - listCloudRelayTasks feeds display only; no authority decision reads it.

author: Claude
message:
Undo my double-counting, and fix the guard that caused it

I reported that 171 mesh tests "had never executed" and wired 23 files into
test:deterministic to fix it. That was wrong, and the wiring made things worse.

tests/agent-relay.test.mjs imports 19 of those suites, and that file is in
test:deterministic. They were running all along. Naming them as well made them
execute twice, which is why the suite jumped to 1521 -- a number that looked
like progress and was double-counting. Verified by name: the same test titles
appeared twice in the output.

Root cause is my own build-wiring guard. It counted package.json references
only, so any file that runs by import looked orphaned. A verification tool
that is wrong is worse than no tool, because it manufactures confident action
-- which is precisely what it did to me.

Fixed properly:

  - The orphan check now resolves the import graph transitively. A test file
    runs if a script names it OR if something that runs imports it.
  - A second guard catches the inverse mistake: a file both named by a script
    and imported by another script's file executes twice, inflating the pass
    count that a reader trusts and doubling runtime for nothing.
  - The 19 double-listed files are removed from the script. The importing file
    already runs them.

Both directions were checked by deliberately reintroducing each fault: adding
agent-worker-runtime.test.mjs back to the script fails the double-listing
guard by name, and dropping an unreferenced file into tests/ fails the orphan
guard by name.

Verified position: zero test files are orphaned, and none run twice.

The check:syntax additions from that commit stay. node --check does not follow
imports, so covering 25 previously unchecked src modules -- including
security.mjs and crypto.mjs -- was real and is unaffected by this.

Honest numbers now: 1386 tests, 1344 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped. The earlier
1521 was inflated. The report and failure matrix are corrected in this commit
rather than left to read as achievement.

author: Claude
message:
Stop a compute budget rolling back to less spend when snapshot timestamps collide

P0, and the same shape as the execution-record resurrection fixed in the
previous commit -- except the state being rewound here is money.

loadLatestComputeBudget picked the newest snapshot by sorting on wall-clock
alone. Two saves for one budget inside the same millisecond are
indistinguishable to that sort, so the loader could restore an OLDER budget:
less spend recorded, more capacity free.

Measured deterministically by stamping three snapshots with one fixed instant:

  true state : 700 cents committed, 300 available
  loaded     : 0 cents committed, 1000 available

Seven hundred cents of recorded spend vanished and the same capacity
reappeared from nowhere -- on restart, after a crash, exactly when the system
is least able to notice. The value-level conservation property was already
tested and held; nothing tested conservation across persistence, which is
where it actually broke.

committedCostCents and committedTokens only ever increase: commit adds to
them, and neither reserve nor release touches them. So they are a monotonic
ordering key. Snapshots now rank by recorded spend first, then time, then the
store's row sequence, and the newest wins regardless of what the clock says.

Finding this immediately after the execution-record bug is the useful part.
Both were the same mistake in different files: "latest" defined as "most
recently stamped" rather than "furthest along a monotonic quantity". The
remaining time-only sorts in agent-autonomy-store, agent-code-artifact-store
and cloud-agent-relay have the same shape and are recorded in the failure
matrix as unreviewed rather than quietly assumed safe.

author: Claude
message:
Stop a terminal execution being resurrected by two writes in the same millisecond

P0, found by the soak rather than by reading the state machine.

"Latest execution record" was decided by sorting on detail.createdAt, which is
a wall-clock stamp. Two writes for one task inside the same millisecond -- a
fast worker, or any clock coarser than the gap between two saves -- are
indistinguishable to that sort, so the transition guard could compare a new
write against the OLDER record instead of the newest.

Measured, deterministically, by passing one fixed date to three saves:

  MODEL_RESULT_READY   -> saved
  RESULT_SUBMITTED     -> saved
  MODEL_RESULT_READY   -> ACCEPTED, terminal task reopened
  loadLatestAgentExecution -> MODEL_RESULT_READY

The terminal state was not merely bypassed, it was lost. Every guard in
validateExecutionTransition was correct and none of them ran against the right
record.

Ordering now ranks by how far along the state machine a record is, then by
time, then by the store's own row sequence. That puts the monotonicity
invariant into the ordering itself, so a terminal record wins over an earlier
stage whatever the clock says -- which also covers skew, rollback, and
out-of-order delivery, none of which a timestamp sort survives. The sequence
tiebreak compares the numeric tail of the row id, because "row-9" sorts after
"row-12" lexically.

Also adds tests/agent-mesh-soak.test.mjs: 1,000 tasks through the real state
machines with crashes injected at four durable boundaries (before dispatch,
after model success before persistence, after persistence before submission,
after submission before recording it), plus a concurrency race and a direct
resurrection attempt. It asserts each boundary was actually exercised -- a
soak that never crashed proves nothing about crash recovery -- and checks
capacity conservation, no duplicate compute, no lost terminal state, and
bounded audit growth.

That soak is what found this. Reverting the ordering fix fails soak tests 1
and 3; restored, 3/3.

Fail closed when a task declares no consequence class at all

The worker is only permitted to do local preparation, and it checked for that
like this:

  if (task.consequenceClass && task.consequenceClass !== 'LOCAL_PREPARATION')

The guard fires only when a class is PRESENT and wrong. A task that declares

something I am not allowed to do" and "you did not say what you are asking

compiler always declares a class -- so closing it changed no existing
behaviour. The full suite is unchanged at 0 failures.

task must reserve no compute. Failing closed after the reservation would let a

author: Claude
message:
Stop rejecting a crash-recovery replay because its keys arrived in a different order

Terminal idempotency exists so that a crash after the work is done converges
instead of conflicting. The record that comes back on recovery is rebuilt from
persisted pieces, so its fields arrive in whatever order the rebuilding code
emits them -- not necessarily the order they were first written in.

sameExecutionRecord compared with a raw JSON.stringify, which makes key order
part of the identity. Measured: an execution record replayed with identical
facts and reordered keys returned terminal-execution-history-conflict. The
guard rejected the replay on exactly the path it exists to serve.

This branch already had the right answer twenty lines away, in
cloud-agent-relay's canonicalValue/sameJson, written for the same problem in
the relay. Two implementations of "are these the same record" is how one of
them ends up order-sensitive while the other is not, so sameJson is now
exported and reused rather than copied. One canonical primitive.

The comparison is order-insensitive for object keys only. Arrays are left
alone deliberately -- [a,b] and [b,a] are different data, and collapsing them
would hide a real divergence. There is a test for that, alongside tests that a
different provider and different usage numbers are still conflicts. Making a
comparison forgiving must not make it blind.

Verified by reverting to JSON.stringify: the reordered-replay test fails,
3/4 pass. Restored: 4/4.

author: Claude
message:
Let a safely-released compute task try again, and prove capacity is conserved

Found by attacking the budget rather than reading it.

P1: a released reservation permanently blocked its own retry. reserveCompute
refused any taskId present in the reservation map, which lumps together three
situations that need different answers:

  RESERVED  -- live. Reserving again lets two workers spend one allocation.
  COMMITTED -- compute was already bought under this identity. Reserving again
               is how you pay twice for one task.
  RELEASED  -- capacity handed back, NO provider call made (rate limited,
               cancelled before dispatch). Nothing to double-spend.

Only the first two are double-spend risks. Refusing the third strands the task
forever: the budget reports full capacity and that task can never touch it, so
the safe-retry path -- the one for failures known not to have executed -- did
not exist. Measured before fixing: reserve, release, retry -> refused, with
1000/1000 cents available.

Now RELEASED may be re-reserved and the earlier attempt is carried forward as
attempt/priorReservationIds rather than overwritten, so the history stays
readable. RESERVED and COMMITTED are refused exactly as before, and there are
tests for both -- loosening one status must not loosen the others.

P2: the reservation cap reported 'reservation-count-limit-reached' whether the
map was full of live reservations or of finished history. Those need opposite
responses from an operator. Terminal records still count toward the bound,
because the map is the audit trail and unbounded growth is a real memory
concern, but the reason code now says which limit was reached.

tests/ai-compute-budget-conservation.test.mjs attacks the invariant that
matters: capacity can be spent, returned, or held, never created. A seeded
3,000-step random walk of reserve/commit/release checks the invariant after
every transition, not just at the end -- a budget that goes briefly wrong and
recovers is still wrong. It asserts the run actually exercised release (>50)
and retry-after-release (>10), because a property test that never reaches the
path it exists for proves nothing.

Verified by reverting the fix: 3 of the 6 new tests fail, including the
conservation walk. Restored: 6/6.

0 fail, 42 skipped.

The ingress had never handled a real request; every test used a fake client.

author: Claude
message:
Fix the HTTP ingress: poll was broken, and receipts lost their provenance

The ingress had never handled a real request. Every test drove it with a fake
client, so nothing had ever exercised the code that builds GitHub URLs or
forwards a submit. Running it once against the real API found two defects.

poll returned 400. The transport passes state 'OPEN'; GitHub answers 422 for
anything but lowercase. The operation ChatGPT uses to discover work at all was
broken against the real API while the unit suite was green -- because every
fake accepted whatever it was handed. Normalised at the client boundary, which
is the layer that has to speak GitHub's dialect, rather than asking each
caller to remember.

Receipt provenance was discarded in silence. Only workerId, status and result
were forwarded, so a caller that carefully supplied sourceCommit, confidence,
findings, limitations and duration got a receipt recording UNKNOWN for all of
them -- and a 200 RECEIVED saying it had worked. Dropping evidence while
reporting success is the worst failure this contract can have. Issue #65
captures it; #66 is the same request afterwards, with every field intact.

The tests now drive the real client through a fake fetch, and the fake behaves
like GitHub instead of accepting anything: it returns 422 for a non-lowercase
state, exactly as the API does. A fake that says yes to everything is not a
test double, it is a way to keep a bug.

One of the new tests exists for a failure mode worse than the 400 -- a
validation error that turns into 200 with count:0, which reads as "no work to
do" when the truth is "the query was rejected". It pins that this fails loudly.

Both regression tests were verified by reverting each fix in turn and
confirming the matching test fails. A test that cannot fail is not protection.

1195 tests, 1153 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped. 13/13 in vercel-agent-relay.

The ingress is still deployed nowhere. This was driven over loopback against
the real GitHub API, which exercises every line except the hosting.

author: Claude
message:
Stop the worker reporting a killed suite as a failure, or a lost result as work done

Two defects, both of the same kind: a failure shaped like a success.

A timed-out suite was reported as a failed one. execFile signals a timeout
kill the same way it signals a non-zero exit, and nothing separated them, so
a suite that never finished produced status FAILED, confidence HIGH,
truthTable FAILED and decision REPAIR. Captured on issue #61: that receipt
asserts the deterministic suite fails. It does not -- it passes 1191 tests.
The receipt claimed a verification result it never obtained, at high
confidence, and asked a reviewer to repair something that is fine. A timeout
now reports NOT_RUN, LOW confidence, OWNER_REQUIRED, and a limitation saying
in plain words that this is not evidence the suite fails.

The first attempt at that fix did not work, and issue #61 is the record of
it. The check tested `error.code === undefined`; Node sets it to `null` on a
timeout kill, so the condition silently never matched and the bug shipped
looking fixed. `killed === true` is the marker. Verified against the real
error object rather than assumed a second time.

A failed submit counted as handled work. `handled += 1` ran unconditionally,
so a result that could not be filed consumed a slot against maxTasks -- the
worker stopped early having accomplished nothing -- and logged at normal
level as though the task were done. What actually follows is the lease
lapsing, the task stranding, and one of its three attempts spent on work that
was completed and thrown away. It now logs SUBMIT FAILED at error level,
counts nothing, and exits non-zero so a scheduler notices instead of
recording a clean run.

Also corrected a claim I made when proposing this work: a stale poll snapshot
is NOT a bug. claimGithubRelayTask re-reads the issue and its comments and
refuses with task-already-completed, so the claim is the authority and the
snapshot cannot cause duplicate work. Checked before building anything.

author: Claude
message:
Renew the lease while a suite runs, and stop when it is gone

The worker never heartbeated. A suite runs for minutes; the lease is finite.
Nothing renewed it, so a slow machine or a longer suite would let it lapse
mid-run, another worker would take the task, and this one would finish, try
to submit, and be told lease-owner-mismatch -- every minute of work discarded
with no message anyone would think to look for. It happened to fit today
because check:syntax takes 16 seconds against a 1800-second lease. That is
margin, not a design.

It now renews once a minute while a suite runs (configurable via
RELAY_HEARTBEAT_MS), and if a renewal is REFUSED it kills the child rather
than spending the remaining minutes producing a result it cannot submit. A
transient network error is not treated as a lost lease: only an explicit
refusal counts, because the two are not the same and guessing wrong throws
away good work.

Both branches proved live, not in fixtures.

Renewal: `test:deterministic` (~2 min) with a 20-second interval renewed the
lease 5 times and completed normally (issue #57).

Abort: the obvious test could not work. A rival submitted a competing result
40 seconds into a run and was REFUSED with lease-owner-mismatch, because an
actively heartbeating worker still holds a live lease (issue #58). That is

author: Claude
message:
Let the worker actually reach the recovery path, and emit a real receipt

Two defects in the unattended worker, both found by running it against a
genuinely stranded task rather than by reading it.

The recovery path was unreachable. The worker filtered candidates on
`!task.claimed`, but `claimed` means only "the agent-relay:claimed label is
present" -- and that label stays on a task whose worker died holding the
lease. Abandoned tasks were therefore invisible to the one process able to
rescue them. Lease recovery was shipped, tested, and could never once have
run in production.

It now considers already-claimed tasks too and lets claimGithubRelayTask
decide, because that function reads the real lease from the comments and is
the only authority on whether one is live. Fresh work still goes first;
recovery is what a worker does when there is nothing new. Verified end to
end: a task abandoned by `dead-worker` was picked up on the next run as
"attempt 2/3", executed, and answered. The same run before this change
reported "0 unclaimed" and exited.

The receipts were hollow. The worker filled in none of the fourteen mandated
fields, so the only unattended producer in the system emitted the weakest
evidence in it: sourceCommit UNKNOWN, confidence UNKNOWN, no limitations. A
receipt that cannot name the commit it describes is not evidence of anything.
It now resolves the commit once per run and reports real commands, tests,
duration, findings and limitations.

Confidence is HIGH only when a suite actually ran to completion. An
unsupported objective produced no evidence at all, so claiming confidence in
it would be precisely the dishonesty the receipt contract exists to prevent.

Proof receipt on issue #55: sourceCommit 43445c2, confidence HIGH, duration
16628ms, command "npm run check:syntax", 2 limitations, 16 fields,
validateRelayReceipt returns no reason codes.

author: Claude
message:
Recover abandoned tasks visibly, and stop retrying the ones that keep killing workers

An expired lease was already claimable again -- that is the recovery path and
it is correct. Two things were wrong with how it worked.

It was silent. A worker took over an abandoned task and the thread read as
though the first attempt never happened, which is precisely the history
someone debugging a repeatedly-failing task needs. A takeover now says so in
the comment and carries recoveredFrom/lapsedAt in the packet, and the claim
returns CLAIMED_RECOVERED rather than CLAIMED.

It was unbounded. A task that kills whatever picks it up got handed to worker
after worker forever, burning one per cycle while the issue list showed
healthy-looking activity -- a crash loop wearing a queue as a costume. Claims
are now capped (default 3, configurable) and refuse with
task-exceeded-max-attempts past it.

Order matters and is tested: the attempt cap is checked AFTER the live-lease
guard, so a task under its limit can never let a second worker barge in on a
lease that is still alive.

Proved against real GitHub on issue #52, not fixtures -- three one-second
leases stranding in sequence, each takeover naming the worker it recovered
from, the fourth refused.

That proof exposed a follow-on gap worth as much as the feature. A task at
the cap is stranded permanently, and relay-status reported it identically to
one a worker would happily retry -- telling the reader to run another worker,
the one action that cannot work. EXHAUSTED is now a distinct verdict that
outranks STRANDED and says to read the claim history instead. The worker
likewise distinguishes GIVING UP from an ordinary skip; logging both as
"skipped" hid the difference exactly when it mattered.

author: Claude
message:
Make the relay say what it is doing

The GitHub issue list cannot answer "is the relay working?". An issue
labelled agent-relay:claimed looks identical whether a worker is mid-run or
died an hour ago holding the lease. A queue with nothing running looks
identical to a queue being worked. Those need opposite responses.

summarizeRelayQueue() separates the four states that actually differ:

  IDLE      nothing to do
  ACTIVE    work waiting or in flight, someone is on it
  STALLED   work waiting and nothing running. Not broken -- nobody is home,
            which is the easiest failure to mistake for a crash.
  STRANDED  a worker claimed a task and vanished. The lease lapsed so the task
            is claimable again, but work may have been done and thrown away
            and nothing announces that.

STRANDED outranks STALLED deliberately: idle means nobody started, stranded
means someone started and disappeared.

It is a pure function over issues, comments and `now`, so it is testable
without a network and cannot drift from what the transport reports.
scripts/relay-status.mjs is a thin read-only wrapper that exits 1 on
STRANDED or STALLED, so it can gate a check without anyone parsing output.

Proved against real GitHub, not fixtures: opened issue #50, claimed it with a
one-second lease so it would strand immediately, and the report caught it.
That run exposed a gap worth more than the feature -- it printed "last held
by null", because resolveLease() threw away the claimant once a lease
expired. For a stranded task that is the single fact you need: which worker
vanished. lastHolder and lapsedAt are now preserved. holder stays null,
because nobody holds an expired lease and existing callers branch on that, so
the new fields cannot change any current decision.

Issue #50 is closed with an explanation of why it existed.

author: Claude
message:
Tell mechanical merge conflicts apart from real ones, automatically

The same twenty-minute ritual kept repeating: make a throwaway worktree,
merge main, stare at the conflicts, work out whether they are real, run the
suite, write it up. Three times in one week -- and twice out of three the
answer was "both sides appended to the same list".

git already says whether a branch conflicts. What it cannot say is whether
the conflict MATTERS, and those two cases look identical in a status output
while needing completely different responses:

  MECHANICAL   both sides added in the same place. A union resolves it and
               nothing is lost. Nobody needs to think.
  NEEDS_HUMAN  the sides changed the same thing to different values. One has
               to win, and only a person can say which.

scripts/pr-reconcile.mjs classifies every open PR in one command. It is
read-only: it never pushes, never writes to a branch, and removes every
worktree it creates. Running the suite is opt-in because it is slow.

What it says about the queue right now, and this took one command rather
than an afternoon:

  #45  MECHANICAL   package.json script lists only
  #40  CLEAN        no conflict at all
  #7   NEEDS_HUMAN  store.mjs -- both sides evolved the same schema in
                    different directions, PR at version 9 with
                    sourceEvidence/opportunities, main at version 6 with
                    providerEvents/leadLists. That is a versioning decision,
                    not a merge.
  #5   NEEDS_HUMAN  11 divergent regions in store.mjs alone, across 10 files

Two bugs found by running it rather than by reading it: a PR head pushed
since the last fetch failed with a bare "invalid reference" that reads like a
broken PR rather than an unfetched ref, and git's stderr from probes that are
*expected* to fail was printing over the report, making a working tool look
broken. Both fixed.

Verified against a case with a known answer: #40 reports CLEAN, and running

author: Claude
message:
Make the build refuse to hide a test that never runs

A test file that exists but is in no npm script is worse than no test: it
looks like coverage, reports nothing, and rots. That is not hypothetical --
an incoming branch added 22 test files without touching package.json, one of
them was failing, and there was no way for anyone to find out. I only caught
it by running the files by hand.

tests/build-wiring.test.mjs closes that hole with four guards, all keyed off
what is actually on disk rather than a maintained list:

  - every tests/*.test.mjs is referenced by some test: script
  - every src/**/*.mjs is in check:syntax
  - test:deterministic references no file that has been deleted
  - test:deterministic lists no file twice

The last two exist because this line is a recurring merge-conflict site --
both sides append to it, and a careless resolution either drops entries or
duplicates them. A dropped entry silently stops running tests; a stale entry
makes the whole suite die on module-not-found before a single test executes,
which reads as catastrophe rather than a bookkeeping slip.

The src guard found 10 modules that check:syntax never covered, including
security.mjs and crypto.mjs -- exactly the files where an unparsed error
should not reach a production start. All 10 parse today; they are now wired
in, so it stays that way.

Proved the guard by breaking it on purpose: an orphan test file added to
tests/ fails the run and names the file, and passes again once removed. It
also caught itself before it was wired in, which is the correct first catch.

author: Claude
message:
Scan for secrets by type, not by name

This is the third time a compute counter has been rejected as a credential.
maxTokens on a task budget, tokens in receipt cost accounting, and now
coordination.tokenBudget in the autonomy worker -- three names for the same
idea, each caught by /token/i, each a legitimate payload refused.

The first two were fixed by naming them as exceptions. That was treating the
symptom: the rule itself was wrong, and a fourth name was always going to
turn up. It did.

An authentication token is a string. A counter is a number. So a token-shaped
key holding a non-negative integer, or an explicitly unmeasured null, is a
counter and passes -- whatever it is called. A string under the same key still
falls through to the scanner, so a real credential hidden under tokenBudget is
caught exactly as before. The exemption is deliberately limited to /token/i;
password, apikey, secret and friends have no counter meaning and stay blocked
whatever their value.

One assertion changed rather than being quietly dropped: hasSecret({accessToken: 1})
was true and is now false. That is the intended trade, and it is stated in the
test. The integer 1 is not a usable credential, so rejecting it bought no
safety while the strict reading cost three real false positives. What the
scanner exists to stop -- a high-entropy string leaking into a public issue --
is unaffected, and the negative cases now pin that explicitly.

Found by running PR #40's test suite, which is not wired into any npm script
and therefore had never executed. tests/openai-worker-roundtrip.test.mjs was
failing on that branch and nobody could have known.

Verified: 18/18 github-relay, 1134 tests 0 fail repository-wide, and PR #40's
22 orphaned test files go 313/314 -> 314/314 with this change alone.

author: Claude
message:
Collapse five overlapping relay documents into one canonical handoff

There were five documents describing the bridge, written at different times,
disagreeing with each other about what was live. That is worse than having
none: a reader picks whichever one they open first.

docs/LIVE_BRIDGE_HANDOFF.md is now the single handoff document. It covers the
loop end to end -- creating a task, claiming it, leases and heartbeats, the
receipt contract, how the reviewer verifies, when to raise a repair task
instead of retrying, the fail-closed authority boundary, and how to start and
stop a worker. The other five get a one-paragraph banner pointing at it.

Three things it states plainly rather than implying:

- The lease is resolved by earliest server-assigned comment id. That is
  deterministic after the fact but cannot un-run work a losing worker already
  did. GitHub offers no row lock; the Postgres transport does.
- The HTTP ingress returns 503 RELAY_NOT_CONFIGURED and always has. That is
  correct fail-closed behaviour, not a working front door, and it has never
  carried a task. Its current state could not be re-checked from here: the
  connected Vercel account lists zero projects and the egress proxy returns
  403 CONNECT for *.vercel.app. Recorded as unverified, not refuted.
- A message channel is not a capability multiplier. The bridge creates no
  extra Claude usage and bypasses no subscription. Tasks sit in the queue
  until something is running to claim them.

The owner action card is one card, five minutes, and optional -- the bridge
already works over GitHub Issues without it. It names the exact permissions
(Metadata read, Issues read/write, fine-grained, this repository only) and
the three environment variable names, and no values.

ran against, what actually executed, or what the worker could not check.

Expand the receipt contract from 6 fields to the full 14: taskId, workerId,
status, sourceCommit, commands, tests, artifacts, findings, limitations,
confidence, externalEffects, cost, duration, submittedAt. sourceCommit and
limitations are the two that matter most -- without the first a receipt is
unanchored, and without the second a partially blocked task reads as a clean
pass. validateRelayReceipt() rejects anything missing, any unrecognised
confidence level, and any receipt claiming a nonzero external effect.

Add githubRelayTaskEnvelope(), which derives status, lease, attempt count,
result refs and idempotency key from the issue and its comments. Deriving it
means there is no second copy of the truth to drift out of sync with GitHub.

Fix two secret-scanner false positives found by running the scanner against
real payloads rather than fixtures:

- cost.tokens is a compute-unit counter, not an authentication token, but the
  key name alone was enough to trip the scan. Exempt it only when the value
  is null or a non-negative integer.
- externalEffects.credentialChanges tripped the scan because the zero-ledger
  exemption covered externalEffectLedger and not externalEffects. Both names
  carry the identical shape, so both get the exemption.

Both were real: they blocked legitimate receipts, which is the failure mode
that quietly teaches people to bypass the scanner.

author: Claude
message:
Make the relay worker actually work unattended, and prove it on a real task

The device-off path was staged but had never run. Running it surfaced two
defects that a green test suite could not, and both would have made the
"device-off" claim false in practice.

DEFECT 1 - Node's fetch silently ignores HTTPS_PROXY.
curl and git honour proxy env vars automatically; Node 22's global fetch does
not unless NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1. In a proxied environment the proxy is what
carries the usable credential, so every GitHub API call from the worker
returned 401 while an identical curl returned 201. Measured side by side:

  curl via proxy                   -> 201
  curl --noproxy '*'               -> 401
  node fetch (default)             -> 401
  node fetch NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1  -> 200

The worker now re-execs once with the flag when a proxy is configured, and is
untouched on an ordinary host where none exists.

DEFECT 2 - that failure would have stranded a real task.
Claim happens before the work, so a credential failing on first write fails
AFTER the claim comment has landed, leaving a genuine task locked under a lease
held by an already-dead worker until it expires. Added a GET /user credential
preflight that refuses to claim anything if it fails. One request removes the
whole class of outage.

PROVEN UNATTENDED, on a task this worker did not author:
issue #32 ("Verify Vercel relay ingress") was created by a different agent and
handled end to end by scripts/github-relay-worker.mjs with only Bash and the
environment credential - no MCP tools, no human, no GitHub Actions, no Vercel.
It authenticated, polled, claimed #32, ran npm run test:deterministic to
completion, posted a result receipt with a strictly-zero effect ledger, and
closed the issue.

capability-graph: github-relay-transport promoted to VERIFIED_LIVE. That status
had to be ADDED to CAPABILITY_STATUSES, because nothing in UberBond had ever
earned it before - everything was tested-but-never-run or run-but-unproven. A
regression test now guards it: a VERIFIED_LIVE claim must cite an externally
addressable artifact (issue number, receipt, deployment), not just prose.

Still not proven, and said so in the docs: the hourly Routine that fires this
worker has not yet fired on its own schedule, and the GitHub Actions workflow
remains unexecuted while Actions is blocked on this account.

author: Claude
message:
Make the ChatGPT<->Claude Code bridge actually live, over GitHub Issues

The relay was blocked on a deployed HTTP host that does not exist. That was
treated as "no live bridge is possible." It wasn't: the mission's own Wave 5
listed a GitHub-mediated task packet as an available path, and GitHub is
already a durable, authenticated, always-on store both ends can reach with no
new host and no new spend.

src/github-relay.mjs implements that transport, and it has now carried a real
task end to end on real infrastructure (issue #30):

  producer opens issue #30 (label agent-relay:task, fenced uberbond-task packet)
    -> worker polls, claims under a 1800s lease (comment 5348571058)
    -> worker runs real bounded work: npm run test:deterministic
       => 1092 tests, 1050 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped, exit 0
    -> worker posts a uberbond-result receipt (comment 5348593358)
    -> issue labelled agent-relay:done and closed

No mock at any hop. Real issue, real comment ids, real timestamps, real
measured numbers.

A REAL DEFECT THE LIVE RUN FOUND, that no fixture could:
issue bodies come back HTML-escaped through some GitHub clients (`"` as
`"`), so JSON.parse failed and the relay reported zero claimable tasks
while a valid task sat open -- a silent, total failure of the bridge. Worse,
the escaping is inconsistent between endpoints on the same client: the issue
body was escaped, its comments were not. extractFencedJson now tries raw and
falls back to single-pass entity decoding (single-pass so a literal
"&#34;" is never double-decoded into a quote), with regression tests for
both directions.

Same contract, different wire -- not a second relay: this module imports
ZERO_EFFECTS, hasSecret(), and validResult() from cloud-agent-relay.mjs and
compiles packets with the same compileAgentTask(), so the two transports
cannot drift on what they consider safe. A result claiming any nonzero
external effect is rejected identically on both.

Also staged for unattended, device-off operation:
- scripts/github-relay-worker.mjs -- runs ONLY three allowlisted npm scripts
  and reports UNSUPPORTED_OBJECTIVE otherwise; it never executes free text
  from an issue body, because "anyone who can open an issue" must not mean
  "anyone who can run code in CI".
- .github/workflows/agent-relay-worker.yml -- fires on issues opened/labeled
  plus an hourly cron, concurrency-guarded, permissions limited to
  issues:write + contents:read.

Status is honestly LIVE_UNPROVEN, not VERIFIED_LIVE: the one live run was
driven by an interactive session acting as the worker. The unattended path has
never executed because GitHub Actions on this account is failing at the
infrastructure level -- CI ran clean through 2026-07-17, then every run from
fe51c3c onward dies in ~3-10s with 404 job logs, which dates it to an Actions
billing/quota lapse rather than the code.

Honest limitation recorded in the module, the capability graph, and the docs:
GitHub labels and comments are not database row locks. resolveLease() resolves
a race deterministically after the fact (earliest server-assigned comment id
wins, same answer regardless of asker or comment order) but cannot prevent
duplicated work that already happened. Fine for a few owner-initiated tasks
and one worker; not for high concurrency. cloud-agent-relay.mjs, with real
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED proven against a real PostgreSQL server,
stays the transport to promote once a real host exists.

Full local gate: 1092 tests, 1050 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped. lite/ untouched.

author: Claude
message:
Audit and harden the governed ChatGPT<->Claude cloud relay (PR #28)

Real, verified defect fixes and gap closures found while auditing the
merged relay (src/cloud-agent-relay.mjs, server.mjs /api/agent-relay/*,
scripts/uberbond-mcp.mjs relay tools) against the mission's Wave 2-4
requirements -- each proven, not asserted:

- Fixed a double-escaped SECRET_VALUE regex (`Bearer\\s+\\S+` inside a
  regex literal matches a literal backslash, never real whitespace) that
  let a raw "Bearer <token>" string past the secret scanner when nested
  under a non-secret-shaped key.
- Fixed an unanchored `sk-`/`ghp_` pattern that false-positived on ordinary
  ids -- found live via the new end-to-end proof, which rejected a normal
  taskId ("e2e-task-1787174626471") because it contains "sk-1787..." as a
  mid-word substring. Anchored both patterns with \b.
- Added the rate limiting the mission's Wave 3 requires (previously
  entirely absent): a sliding one-minute-per-IP limiter on all
  /api/agent-relay/* routes, config.agentRelay.rateLimitPerMinute.
- Added the heartbeat lease-extension the mission's Wave 3/8 require
  (previously entirely absent -- only claim/submit existed): a real
  heartbeatCloudRelayTask() reusing store.heartbeatJob()'s existing
  ownership enforcement, POST /api/agent-relay/tasks/:taskId/heartbeat,
  and the uberbond_relay_heartbeat MCP tool. Without this, any relay task
  running longer than the 5-minute lock timeout risked stale-lease
  reclaim mid-task.
- Added relayHealthSummary() (queued/active/completed/dead-letter counts,
  oldest queued task, stale-lease count) wired into GET
  /api/agent-relay/health, closing the mission's Wave 9 observability gap
  without exposing any task payload.

Real proof obtained this wave (not fake-store-only):
- A real local HTTP server (server.mjs) and a real local MCP process
  (scripts/uberbond-mcp.mjs) driven over actual stdio JSON-RPC, wired
  together over real localhost HTTP: init -> tool list -> poll -> claim ->
  heartbeat -> submit -> rejected replay, with every byte of captured
  process stdout/stderr scanned and confirmed to never contain the raw
  relay token.
- Real embedded PostgreSQL 18 concurrency proof: claimJobsByType's
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED under two workers racing for one relay task,
  excludeTypes protecting relay jobs from normal workers, and
  target-agent isolation (22/22 in tests/postgres-store-live.test.mjs).

author: Claude
message:
Add the Revenue Safety, Recovery, and Audit Foundation

Four coherent subsystems, all reusing canonical models -- no parallel
queue, suppression, evidence, or revenue model was created:

1. Reservation recovery (src/reservation-recovery.mjs): a time-boxed,
   bounded, deterministic sweep for outboundReservations stuck at
   'reserved' or 'dispatching' past a timeout. Reuses the exact
   existing state machine: a stale 'reserved' row (provider never
   reached) is safely cancelled; a stale 'dispatching' row (provider
   outcome genuinely unknown) is reclassified to the existing
   'uncertain' state, which the guard already treats as a permanent
   replay-block -- so a recovered row can never be silently resent.
   No new status, no migration (the status column has no CHECK
   constraint). Concurrent/duplicate sweeps are deduplicated via the
   store's existing duplicate-id ConflictError mechanism rather than a
   bespoke lock, since PostgreSQL doesn't support nesting a second
   transaction inside the caller's.

2. Volume/quota unification: extracted countActiveOutboundReservations()
   into send-safety.mjs as the one canonical daily/hourly cap-counting
   helper. Both evaluateDeliverabilityGuard and
   JsonStore._reserveOutboundSendDirect now call it instead of
   maintaining two independent implementations that could silently
   drift. No limit or threshold changed -- every pre-existing
   send-safety/pipeline test still passes unmodified.

3. Transactional report-email audit: RevenueEngine.sendReportEmail now
   writes a report_email_audit receipt for every decision (kill-switch
   block, missing destination, provider-capability-absent, uncertain
   outcome, sent), and a provider exception sets
   lead.reportEmailAttemptStatus='uncertain' which onProspectComplete's
   auto-send gate now checks to prevent ever automatically retrying an
   unresolved external outcome. Deliberately kept separate from the
   cold-outreach guard, since the destination is self-submitted at
   public intake, not discovered or inferred.

4. Operator visibility (src/outbound-operator-summary.mjs): a read-only
   structured summary of reservation states, a stale-recovery dry-run
   preview, provider health, review requirements, and a deterministic
   next-safe-action string, reusing existing collections only.

standalone as regression checks after each refactor. 198/198 tests
pass in npm run check.
